quests.instruction: Match each word to the meaning that fits.

pairs.value: The top part of your body, above your neck.
The part of your arm used for holding things.
The part of your leg that touches the ground when you stand.

quests.hint: One of these is at the top of you. Two are used for holding or standing.
quests.explanation: Hand and foot are both parts of a limb used for a physical job, one for holding, one for standing. Head is different — it isn't part of a limb at all, and it's where you think, not act.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: The brother of your mother or father.
The sister of your mother or father.
The child of your uncle or aunt.

quests.hint: Two of these are from your parents' generation. One is from yours.
quests.explanation: Uncle and aunt both describe your parents' siblings, one male and one female. Cousin is a generation below both — the child of an uncle or aunt, closer to your own age.

quests.instruction: Match each word to its correct meaning.

pairs.value: The color of blood or a ripe tomato.
The color of a clear sky or the ocean.
The color of a lemon or the sun.

quests.hint: Picture three very different things in nature: one overhead, one on the ground, one above you.
quests.explanation: Red and yellow are both warm colors you'd notice in a sunset, while blue stands apart as a cooler color linked to sky and water.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: The subject that deals with numbers and calculations.
The subject that studies nature and how things work.
The subject where students draw, paint, or create.

quests.hint: Each subject trains a different kind of skill at school.
quests.explanation: Math and science both rely on logic and facts, though one works with numbers and the other with the natural world. Art is different — it's built around creativity, not a single correct answer.

quests.instruction: Match each word to its meaning.

pairs.value: A small number of something.
A large number of something.
An amount that isn't stated exactly.

quests.hint: Two of these tell you roughly how much. One doesn't tell you at all.
quests.explanation: Few and many sit at opposite ends of quantity, one small and one large. Some is different — it doesn't say whether the amount is big or small, only that an amount exists.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its correct meaning.

pairs.value: A round shape with no corners.
A shape with four equal sides and four corners.
A shape with three sides and three corners.

quests.hint: Count the corners on each shape to tell them apart.
quests.explanation: Square and triangle both have straight sides and corners, just a different number of each. A circle has neither — no corners and no straight lines at all.

quests.instruction: Match each word to its meaning.

pairs.value: To request information by questioning someone.
To respond to a question.
To describe something in detail so it's easier to understand.

quests.hint: One of these opens an exchange, one responds to it, and one goes further.
quests.explanation: Ask starts an exchange by requesting information, and answer completes it by responding. Explain goes a step further than a simple answer — it means giving enough detail for real understanding.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: A tool with a blade, used for cutting food.
A tool with a rounded end, used for eating or stirring.
A deep container used for cooking food on a stove.

quests.hint: Two of these you hold while eating or preparing food. One holds the food itself.
quests.explanation: A knife and a spoon are both handheld tools used directly on food, one for cutting and one for scooping. A pot is different — it's a container the food cooks inside, not something you eat with.

quests.instruction: Match each word to its correct meaning.

pairs.value: Any day from Monday to Friday, usually for work or school.
Saturday and Sunday, usually free from work or school.
A day when normal work or school doesn't happen, often for a celebration.

quests.hint: Two of these happen every single week. One happens only sometimes.
quests.explanation: Weekday and weekend divide every week into working days and rest days. A holiday is different — it isn't on a fixed weekly schedule; it's a special day off that can fall on any date.
quests.paragraphTopic: Types of days in a week

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: The direction toward the side where most people's weaker hand is.
The direction toward the side where most people's stronger hand is.
Continuing in the same direction without turning.

quests.hint: Two of these send you sideways in opposite directions. One keeps you going the way you're already facing.
quests.explanation: Left and right point you to opposite sides. Straight is different from both — it means not turning at all, just continuing forward.

quests.instruction: Match each word to its meaning.

pairs.value: A narrow container, usually for liquid, with a cap or lid.
A container with flat sides, often used for storing or shipping things.
A soft container you can carry, often with handles.

quests.hint: One of these is rigid, one is soft, and one is made for liquid.
quests.explanation: A box has flat, rigid sides, while a bag is soft and can bend to fit what's inside. A bottle serves a different purpose entirely — holding liquid without it spilling out.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its correct meaning.

pairs.value: Holding as much as possible, with no room left.
Containing nothing inside.
Containing about fifty percent of what it could hold.

quests.hint: Line these up from nothing inside to no room left.
quests.explanation: Full and empty are opposites, one with no space left and one with nothing inside at all. Half sits exactly between them, holding about as much as it doesn't.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: A small, round piece of metal money.
A piece of paper money.
A small case used for carrying money and cards.

quests.hint: Two of these are types of money. One is where you keep it.
quests.explanation: A coin and a note are both forms of money, just made from different materials. A wallet isn't money at all — it's simply what you carry money in.

quests.instruction: Match each word to its meaning.

pairs.value: To use force to move something away from you.
To use force to move something toward you.
To hold something and move it from one place to another.

quests.hint: Two of these move something in opposite directions. One moves it along with you.
quests.explanation: Push and pull are opposite forces, one sending something away and one bringing it closer. Carry is different from both — you're not pushing or pulling, you're holding something while you move.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its correct meaning.

pairs.value: An open public area with grass and trees, often used for relaxing.
A stretch of sand next to the sea or ocean.
A large area covered with many trees, often wild.

quests.hint: One of these has sand, one has grass and paths, and one is thick with trees.
quests.explanation: A park is a managed green space in or near a town, while a forest is a much wilder area of trees. A beach is different from both — its defining feature is sand next to water, not plants.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: In an early stage of life, not yet old.
No longer young but not yet old, roughly in the middle of life.
Old, especially referring to a person late in life.

quests.hint: Order these three from earliest to latest stage of life.
quests.explanation: Young and elderly sit at opposite ends of a person's life. Middle-aged fills the space between them, the stretch of life that's neither early nor late.

quests.instruction: Match each word to its meaning.

pairs.value: A place where people keep, borrow, or exchange money.
A place where various goods, especially food, are bought and sold.
A place where books are kept for people to read or borrow.

quests.hint: One of these deals with money, one with books, and one with goods for sale.
quests.explanation: A bank handles money and a library handles books — both lend things, just very different things. A market is different from both — it's a place for buying and selling goods directly.
quests.paragraphTopic: Places you'll find in a town

quests.instruction: Match each word with its correct meaning.

pairs.value: Having a lot of weight; hard to lift.
Having little weight; easy to lift.
Easily broken or damaged.

quests.hint: Two of these describe how much something weighs. One describes how easily it breaks.
quests.explanation: Heavy and light are opposites that describe weight. Fragile measures something different — how easily an object breaks, regardless of how much it weighs.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: To repair something that is broken.
To damage something so it no longer works.
To construct something from parts or materials.

quests.hint: One of these damages something, one repairs it, and one creates it from nothing.
quests.explanation: Break and fix are opposite actions, one damages, the other repairs. Build is different from both; it makes something new rather than changing something that already exists.
quests.paragraphTopic: Verbs for repairing and making things

quests.instruction: Match each word to its meaning.

pairs.value: A piece of clothing worn over other clothes to stay warm.
A tool you open above your head to stay dry in the rain.
Clothing worn on the hands to keep them warm or protected.

quests.hint: Two of these protect you from cold. One protects you from rain.
quests.explanation: A coat and gloves both keep parts of your body warm in cold weather. An umbrella serves a different purpose — it isn't clothing, and it protects you from rain, not cold.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its correct meaning.

pairs.value: A plant food, such as a carrot or potato, often eaten as part of a main meal.
Animal flesh eaten as food.
A sweet food eaten at the end of a meal.

quests.hint: Two of these are eaten as part of the main meal. One comes only at the end.
quests.explanation: Vegetables and meat are both usually part of a main course, though one comes from plants and the other from animals. Dessert is different — it's saved for the end, and it's defined by being sweet.

quests.instruction: Match each phrase with its meaning.

pairs.value: A sign showing the way out of a building.
A sign showing the way into a building.
A sign telling people they are not allowed to go in.

quests.hint: Two of these guide you through a doorway. One blocks you from it.
quests.explanation: Exit and entrance are opposite signs, marking the way out and the way in. No entry is different — it isn't directing you anywhere; it's telling you a way is closed.

quests.instruction: Match each phrase with its meaning.

pairs.value: To start a device or machine so it begins working.
To stop a device or machine so it stops working.
To connect a device to a power source using its cord.

quests.hint: One of these connects a device to power. Two describe whether it's running once connected.
quests.explanation: Turn on and turn off are opposite states of a device once it's already connected to power. Plug in comes before either — it's the step that makes the device able to work at all.

quests.instruction: Match each phrase with its meaning.

pairs.value: The date after which food may not taste its best, though it can still be safe.
The list of items used to make a food product.
An instruction to store something in the fridge.

quests.hint: One of these tells you what's inside. Two tell you how or how long to store it.
quests.explanation: Best before and keep refrigerated are both about storage, one gives a time limit, the other a location. Ingredients is different — it tells you what's inside, not how to store it.

quests.instruction: Match each phrase with its meaning.

pairs.value: A greeting used earlier in the day.
A phrase used when saying goodbye, expecting to meet again soon.
A phrase used to show gratitude.

quests.hint: One of these opens a conversation, one closes it, and one expresses appreciation.
quests.explanation: Good morning opens an exchange and see you later closes one, so they sit at opposite points of a conversation. Thank you is different from both — it isn't about timing, it's about gratitude.

quests.instruction: Match each phrase with its meaning.

pairs.value: To stop sleeping.
To rise out of bed after waking.
To lie down in bed in order to sleep.

quests.hint: Two of these happen at the start of the day, in order. One happens at the end.
quests.explanation: Wake up and get up usually happen close together in the morning, first opening your eyes, then leaving the bed. Go to bed is the opposite end of the day, where the routine begins again.
quests.paragraphTopic: Talking about a morning and night routine

quests.instruction: Match each phrase with its meaning.

pairs.value: A short, unspecified amount of time, more than one minute.
Thirty minutes.
The entire day, from start to finish.

quests.hint: Order these from shortest to longest stretch of time.
quests.explanation: A few minutes and half an hour both give a sense of a short wait, though half an hour is a fixed thirty minutes and a few minutes is vaguer. All day is a completely different scale — the whole day, not just part of it.

quests.instruction: Match each phrase with its meaning.

pairs.value: A sign showing that a shop is not currently open for business.
A sign showing that an item is no longer available to buy.
A sign announcing that something will be available in the future.

quests.hint: One of these is about right now, one is about something already run out, and one looks ahead.
quests.explanation: Closed describes the shop's status right now, while sold out describes a specific item that has already run out. Coming soon looks the opposite direction from both — forward, to something not available yet.

quests.instruction: Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.value: Covered in or soaked with liquid.
Free from liquid or moisture.
Slightly wet; not fully dry.

quests.hint: Two of these are opposites. One sits in between them.
quests.explanation: Wet and dry are opposites, one soaked and one with no moisture at all. Damp sits in the middle — not fully dry, but nowhere near as wet as something soaked through.

quests.instruction: Match each phrase with its meaning.

pairs.value: A phrase meaning the speaker has already left and is traveling to meet someone.
A phrase meaning the speaker will return again in a very short time.
A phrase asking someone to wait briefly.

quests.hint: Two of these describe the speaker moving. One asks the listener to pause.
quests.explanation: I'm on my way tells someone you're already traveling, while I'll be right back promises a quick return after leaving. Hold on a second is different from both — it's a request for the listener to simply wait.
